result: Actomyosin rings form initially at the anterior edge of notochord cells and migrate posteriorly to the equator during cell elongation. Before convergent/extension (11.5 hpf), actin is uniformly distributed in the basal cortex. During cell intercalation (16.5 hpf), actin patches appear at the anterior pole, which then connect into a complete ring (17 hpf). Time-lapse recordings show this anterior ring relocates to the equator as cells elongate, with the distance between the anterior pole and ring increasing steadily while the posterior distance remains minimal. Both actin and myosin rings follow this migration pattern, and ring width increases during the process.
evaluation: Claims C21-C30 are well-supported by direct imaging evidence shown in Figures 1D-F and supplementary figures, with quantitative measurements of ring position and width over time. Time-lapse recordings (Video 1) directly demonstrate the continuous migration from anterior to equator. The observations are consistent across multiple markers (Lifeact-mEGFP, mCherry-UtrCH, mCherry-MRLC) and include appropriate quantification with error bars.

result: Blebbistatin treatment prevents ring migration and causes anterior shift of established equatorial rings. When applied at the onset of elongation, blebbistatin prevents both cell elongation and posterior relocation of the actin ring, keeping it at the anterior end. When applied to cells with established equatorial rings, the ring migrates anteriorly at 91.8 ± 10.5 nm/min in a dose-dependent manner, mirroring the reverse of normal development. The effect is reversible upon washing. Ring width remains constant during anterior shift until contacting the lateral domain, after which the posterior edge continues moving anteriorly at 191.6 ± 21.4 nm/min until the ring disappears.
evaluation: Claims C31-C45 are strongly supported by extensive time-lapse imaging data (Figures 1G-H, 2A-D, Videos 2), quantitative measurements of ring position and velocity with appropriate sample sizes (n=10) and statistical significance (p<0.0001), and demonstration of reversibility. The dose-dependence and detailed kinetics strengthen the conclusions. Cell length measurements confirm the ring movement is not due to overall cell shape changes.

result: Talin responds to cortical repositioning rather than driving it, and not all ring components shift with blebbistatin treatment. Live imaging shows talin concentrates at the equator after the ring is established. During blebbistatin treatment, cortical actin shifts to the anterior pole while talin remains at the equatorial position, indicating differential behavior of ring components.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by live imaging data and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing differential localization of actin and talin during blebbistatin treatment. The temporal sequence (talin arrives after ring formation) supports the inference that talin responds to rather than drives ring positioning. However, the claim notes "data not shown" for the initial observation, which is a minor weakness.

result: During blebbistatin treatment, actin filament bundles continue to flow toward the equator but at progressively reduced velocities. In the first 15 min, filament velocity is 7.62 ± 0.78 nm/s (significantly slower than 29.92 nm/s in controls, p<0.001), decreasing further to 3.92 ± 0.9 nm/s in the next 15 min (p=0.004). This deceleration causes trajectory flattening in kymographs, with angles reducing from 39° to 3° within 30 min. After 31.1 ± 1.36 min, directed movement toward the center ceases. No statistical difference exists between anterior- and posterior-directed filament bundles.
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 are well-supported by kymograph analysis (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) with appropriate sample sizes (n=18-22), statistical testing, and quantitative angle measurements. The progressive nature of the effect and symmetry between anterior and posterior flows strengthen the conclusions. The data directly validate the model's predictions about cortical flow dynamics.

result: FRAP experiments reveal differential recovery kinetics in control versus blebbistatin-treated cells. Control embryos show single-exponential recovery with a turnover rate of 90 s ± 3 s. In blebbistatin-treated cells, fluorescence still recovers but with two characteristic times: a fast component similar to controls and a much slower component of 7.8 ± 0.6 min, indicating persistent cortical flow despite reduced myosin activity.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by FRAP data in Figure 2G with appropriate curve fitting and quantification. The two-component recovery in blebbistatin-treated cells is well-explained by the combination of local polymerization/depolymerization (fast) and reduced flow-induced recovery (slow). The 7.8 min slow recovery time matches theoretical predictions based on measured velocity changes, providing strong validation.

result: Prolonged blebbistatin treatment (>1 hr) causes complex ring dynamics with sequential ring formation. The first ring disappears after 106.67 ± 6.06 min, and a second ring emerges at the equator with minimal temporal overlap. The second ring has a significantly shorter dwelling time (61.33 ± 7.81 min, p=0.001). Moving rings are associated with morphological bulges rather than constrictions, and new constrictions form in the wake of shifting rings. In some cells, a third ring emerges after the second disappears.
evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figures 2H-J, Videos 3-4) and kymograph analysis (Figure 2I) with quantitative measurements and statistical testing. The observation of multiple sequential rings and dissociation between rings and constrictions is intriguing and well-documented. However, the mechanism underlying this complex behavior is not fully explained, suggesting additional factors beyond the simple model.

result: Comparative analysis in Halocynthia roretzi demonstrates that nuclear position does not influence ring dynamics. H. roretzi notochord follows similar development to Ciona but with centrally positioned nuclei. Despite this difference, equatorial actomyosin rings form and blebbistatin treatment causes anterior ring shift, indicating nuclear position is not determinative of ring behavior.
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are supported by imaging data from H. roretzi (Figure 3A-G) showing similar ring formation and blebbistatin response despite different nuclear positioning. This comparative approach effectively tests the role of nuclear position. The inference that nuclear position doesn't influence ring dynamics (C73) is well-supported by the parallel behavior in the two species with different nuclear localizations.

result: PCP is not required for equatorial ring positioning but is essential for directional ring movement upon blebbistatin treatment. In wild-type C. savignyi, rings are equatorial with posterior nuclei, and blebbistatin causes anterior shift. In aimless mutants (prickle deletion), 92% of mock-treated cells have equatorial rings despite random nuclear positioning, demonstrating PCP-independent ring positioning. However, blebbistatin treatment of aimless cells causes randomized ring movement (56% equatorial, 18% anterior, 26% posterior, n=57) independent of nuclear position, demonstrating that PCP directs ring movement when contractility is reduced.
evaluation: Claims C74-C83 are strongly supported by genetic analysis using aimless mutants (Figure 4A-E) with appropriate quantification and sample sizes. The dissociation between ring positioning (PCP-independent) and directional movement (PCP-dependent) is clearly demonstrated. The randomization of ring position in blebbistatin-treated aimless mutants provides strong evidence for the tug-of-war model between contractility and PCP.

result: A biophysical model based on active gel theory explains ring formation and positioning through contractility-driven self-organization. The model predicts that local increases in actomyosin concentration create higher contractile stress, leading to a self-reinforcing loop where surrounding fibers flow toward accumulations, opposed by depolymerization and diffusion. Experimental validation shows basal tension increases 2.5-fold during elongation and 1.5-fold during ring migration (measured via angle changes). PIV analysis reveals a robust negative linear correlation between local velocity gradients and actin concentration, validating the model's prediction that flows are driven by actomyosin concentration differences.
evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are supported by theoretical modeling grounded in established active gel theory (cited to Recho et al., 2013) and experimental validation through angle measurements (Figure 5B) and PIV analysis (Figure 5C-D). The negative linear correlation between velocity gradients and actin concentration (C89) provides quantitative validation of the model's key equation. The measurements are appropriately quantified with sample sizes (n>15 for angles).

result: The biophysical model quantitatively reproduces experimental observations of ring dynamics. The model predicts a transition between central ring position (high contractility) and anterior position (low contractility with PCP flux dominance). It reproduces velocity and intensity profiles at late elongation stages (Figure 5E), predicts ring position dynamics during normal migration and blebbistatin treatment (Figure 6B), and predicts linear scaling of ring width with cell length (Figure 6C), all in excellent quantitative agreement with experimental data. The model also accurately predicts actin velocity decay during blebbistatin treatment (Figure 6E).
evaluation: Claims C93-C101 are strongly supported by extensive quantitative comparisons between model predictions and experimental data across multiple independent measurements (Figures 5E, 6B-E). The model successfully predicts dynamics, spatial profiles, and scaling relationships using parameters fixed from independent measurements. The excellent agreement across diverse observables without parameter fitting for each comparison provides strong validation of the model's mechanistic basis.

result: Model simulations and experimental observations support a tug-of-war between contractility and PCP. Simulations predict that without polarity but with high contractility (aimless mutant), rings form centrally, while with low contractility and random polarity (aimless + blebbistatin), rings position randomly. Experimentally, Disheveled initially accumulates basally but relocates to lateral domains with 28% ± 9% anterior enrichment (n=11), occurring at the same time as anterior ring appearance (19-20 hpf). This supports the model's prediction of PCP-driven preferential anterior polymerization that is antagonized by contractility.
evaluation: Claims C102-C106 are supported by model predictions (Figure 7A) that match experimental observations in aimless mutants, and by Disheveled localization data (Figure 7B) with appropriate quantification. The temporal correlation between Disheveled relocation and ring appearance (C105) supports the mechanistic link. The integration of theoretical predictions with genetic and localization data provides strong support for the tug-of-war mechanism.

result: Actomyosin contractility and PCP interact in a tug-of-war to self-assemble and reposition actomyosin rings essential for notochord cell elongation. Rings always form at the anterior edge before migrating to the center as contractility increases, reflecting a novel dynamical property. Contractility localizes cortical flows toward the equator while PCP tries to reposition them anteriorly.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental and theoretical evidence detailed in the other result groups. The tug-of-war mechanism is demonstrated through blebbistatin experiments (reducing contractility causes anterior shift), aimless mutant analysis (loss of PCP randomizes movement), comparative studies (ruling out nuclear position effects), and quantitative modeling that reproduces all observations. The integration of multiple experimental approaches with theoretical modeling provides strong support.

result: Background on Ciona notochord structure and function. The notochord consists of 40 post-mitotic cells in a single file that elongate from coin-shaped to drum-shaped. An actomyosin contractile ring at the basal equator produces circumferential constriction, transmitting force through incompressible cytoplasm to drive elongation. The ring is maintained by bi-directional cortical flow with constant turnover similar to cytokinetic rings. Ring position influences cell shape, as shown by α-actinin mutants. Cells acquire A/P polarity with posterior nuclei and anterior prickle localization.
evaluation: Claims C8-C20 provide established background information supported by cited literature (Cloney 1964, Miyamoto and Crowther 1985, Jiang and Smith 2007, Dong et al. 2009, 2011, Sehring et al. 2014, Jiang et al. 2005, Newman-Smith et al. 2015) and figures showing cell morphology and protein localization. These are well-established facts about the system that provide necessary context for the novel findings.

result: Methodological validation and comparison to cytokinesis. The equatorial ring in notochord cells is established in a spindle-independent manner despite resemblance to cytokinetic rings, as cells are post-mitotic. Lifeact-mEGFP and mCherry-UtrCH bind endogenous actin without interfering with dynamics and show the same localization as endogenous protein in Ciona.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by the post-mitotic nature of notochord cells (inference from established facts) and cited literature validating the actin markers (Burkel et al. 2007, Riedl et al. 2008, Sehring et al. 2014). These provide important methodological validation and conceptual framing but are not primary novel findings.
